Room I

The Laws

The forces that govern love

Exhibit A — Centerpiece

The God of Small Things — Arundhati Roy

History's fiends returned to claim them. To re-wrap them in its old, scarred pelt and drag them back to where they really lived. Where the Love Laws lay down who should be loved. And how. And how much.

Working class women, Malabar, Kerala

The Love Laws in Kerala govern who should be loved and how much. Notably, lower class Paravans were banned from being in any kind of relationship with those of higher classes. These laws are based on caste systems in India the highest being priests, warriors and land owners and the lowest being working class peoples. Placard I.A

Exhibit B

Train to Pakistan — Khushwant Singh

"Something is happening in the village. My father will wake up and know I have gone out. He will kill me." Juggut Singh was not listening to her. That did not bother him as much as the trouble the girl would be in. She might not come again.

Destruction during the Partition of India, 1947

Nooran is scared for her safety. She places precedence on her father's opinion because if they are both discovered together they will face social scrutiny. Crucially, during the Partition, the war between India and Pakistan, Muslims and Hindu Sikhs fought violently. Being caught together breaks the laws in Mano Majra, fueling more tension between the two religions. Placard I.B

Room II

The Love

What made it rebellious

Exhibit A — Centerpiece

Train to Pakistan — Khushwant Singh

Nooran played her last card. "I cannot leave. Jugga has promised to marry me."

A Punjabi family, rural Punjab

Nooran and Jugga's love is sealed with a promise. Their love is pure yet surrounded by the chaos that is the Partition. Placard II.A

Exhibit B

The God of Small Things — Arundhati Roy

At least not until the Terror took hold of him. Not until he saw, night after night, a little boat being rowed across the river. Not until he saw it return at dawn. Not until he saw what his Untouchable son had touched. More than touched. Entered. Loved.

Periyar River, Kerala — the river Ammu and Velutha cross to meet

The quote above is stated by Velutha's father. The "terror" that he feels is like a disease that takes a "hold of him." The Love Laws name Velutha and Ammu's love as dangerously infectious. However, it is also pure with physical "touch." yet that touch turns into terror because of the laws that shape the environment around them. The river represents the space where Ammu and Velutha meet, a symbol for the love that flows despite the laws. Placard II.B

Room III

The Destruction

How love was lost

Exhibit A — Centerpiece

Train to Pakistan — Khushwant Singh

The man's body slid off the rope, but he clung to it with his hands and chin. He pulled himself up, caught the rope under his left armpit, and again started hacking with his right hand. There was a volley of shots. The man shivered and collapsed. The rope snapped in the centre as he fell. The train went over him, and went on to Pakistan.

Refugees crowding a train during the Partition, 1947

The "ghost trains" carry Muslims and Sikhs to be killed. Juggut is the man who stands in front of the train. The train moves continuously showing how the violence it holds is inevitable. Yet, Juggut acts as a physical being trying to stop the violence. Nooran is in that train. Juggut risks his life to save her, a testimony to the love he has for her. But the fact that he stands in front of the train despite its movement shows that there is nothing that can be done, he must die and their love must fail even if he saves her along the way. Placard III.A

Exhibit B

The God of Small Things — Arundhati Roy

Someone switched off the light and Velutha disappeared.

The History House, Ayemenem — sanctuary and symbol of forbidden love

The following photo is the history house, which is the home that Velutha lives in and acts as a sanctuary for the love to thrive, yet is abandoned once Velutha is killed. "Someone" switches the lights off. Velutha's death is not an accident, but was planned. Something could have been done, by anyone to stop it. Their love's destruction was purely intentional. Placard III.B

Room IV

The Grief

What failure leaves behind

Exhibit A — Centerpiece

Train to Pakistan — Khushwant Singh

The whole train could be seen clearly against the wan moonlight. From the coal-tender to the tail end, there was a solid crust of human beings on the roof.

Refugee women and children during the Partition, 1947

The following photo is of the refugees escaping India, with grief. The train carries the physical bodies of humans. The citizens must watch around with nothing left to do. The human bodies decompose just as the people lose hope to be able to do anything about it. Placard IV.A

Exhibit B

The God of Small Things — Arundhati Roy

Mammachi provided the passion. Baby Kochamma the Plan. Kochu Maria was their midget lieutenant. They locked Ammu up before they sent for Velutha. They knew that they had to get him to leave Ayemenem before Chacko returned.

The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden — Benjamin West

The following painting is called The Expulsion from the Garden of Eden painted by Benjamin West. Adam and Eve are the epitomy of choice. Their single act of disobedience is what creates years of suffering. In the same way, Baby Kochamma and Mammachi both make choices that impact the lives of the people they are supposed to love, their child Ammu. In this way, small actions can create catastrophic consequences. Placard IV.B
